source.title: Learning under noisy supervision is governed by a feedback-truth gap

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including main text, figures, extended data, methods, and supplementary information, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own noisy-label training and validation-gap measurements, but its outcome is a feedback–truth gap rather than the original random-label fitting and test-error measures.
record.gate_note: The study tests noisy-label gap dynamics, not the claim’s specific outcomes of zero training error on completely random image labels, chance test error, or preserved generalization on true labels. Its architecture and noise-robust-method comparisons measure gap suppression; they do not establish whether those methods prevent fitting random labels.
record.test_reason: The study reports training–validation gaps under partial label noise, gap suppression, and associations with accuracy. These measures do not establish complete random-label fitting, optimization time, perfect fitting across corruption rates, or learning real patterns before noise. It cites the original findings but tests a related measurement framework.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors argue that a feedback–truth gap follows from faster feedback integration than truth evaluation. They interpret growing dense-network gaps as memorization, architectural constraints as suppression, and human trajectories as active recovery. These are their interpretations of gap measures; the network results do not directly establish the six random-label claim versions.
record.recipe_differences: Measures training-minus-validation accuracy gaps under partial label noise on tabular datasets, with architecture and training-method comparisons; does not reproduce the original random-label image experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Gap prevalence and magnitude vary with label-noise rate and architecture; sparse-residual bottleneck strength α changes gap magnitude and onset. The relationship between gap and validation accuracy differs between dense and sparse-residual networks and weakens under natural CIFAR-10N noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Training–validation gaps grow under partial synthetic label noise, exceed the measurable-gap threshold in over 90% of conditions at 40% noise, and reportedly disappear with clean labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Partial synthetic label noise commonly produces training–validation accuracy gaps in the tested tabular networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse-residual scaffolding, co-teaching, and loss correction reduce gap metrics relative to the dense baseline, with residual gaps on some datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural and training interventions can suppress training–validation gap metrics under partial label noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger gap metrics are associated with lower validation accuracy, with a weaker correlation in sparse-residual networks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The association between training–validation gaps and held-out accuracy depends on architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Accuracy varies with bottleneck strength, and sparse bottlenecks outperform the dense baseline on 93% of datasets at 40% noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse-residual capacity constraints can improve held-out accuracy under partial label noise, with performance depending on constraint strength.

record.problems: The machine-learning core experiments use five selected tabular benchmarks; results on 30 OpenML datasets are summarized in aggregate. The stated code URL is a placeholder (“upon acceptance”), and no confidence intervals are given for several reported gap summaries. The study does not report the original claim’s complete-random-label fitting or chance test-error outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Other reported human, EEG, two-timescale-model, pharmacological, and developmental results do not bear on the claim versions about deep-network fitting of random labels.

untested.parts: Complete random labeling, zero or near-zero training error, chance test error, and fitting without changing architecture or hyperparameters.
Training time relative to true labels and convergence slowdown as corruption increases. Gap-onset time is a different quantity.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit throughout a corruption sweep from none to all and steady test-error degradation toward chance.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent complete random-label fitting, and whether removing them harms generalization on true labels.
Direct comparison of learning shared real-data patterns with memorizing corrupted or random labels over training.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to the supplied claim versions, rather than denials of the reported gap findings. The five core tabular datasets were selected because memorization was observable under 40% noise. A training–validation gap alone cannot distinguish clean-signal learning from noisy-label memorization.

versions.untested_parts: It uses synthetic noisy labels, including 40% noise, on tabular datasets; it does not report fitting a completely random labeling to zero or near-zero training error, chance test error, or unchanged original image-model settings.
Training time or convergence time for random versus true labels, and convergence as corruption increases, are not reported.
Shuffled pixels, permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs are not tested.

The paper measures training-minus-validation accuracy gaps at selected noise settings and reports gap prevalence, but does not report perfect training fit across corruption levels from none to all or a steady test-error trajectory toward chance.

Label smoothing, L2 regularization, and other noise-robust methods are compared on gap metrics under noisy labels; the study does not test whether they prevent fitting random labels or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
The study does not compare the timing of learning shared real-data patterns with the timing of memorizing noise or random labels.

rows.subject: unregularized dense neural network
rows.operation_detail: Trained on tabular data with 40% label noise; training-minus-validation accuracy gap measured over epochs.
rows.value: The gap persists and grows throughout training with no sign of self-correction.
rows.locator: Figure 1a caption; Results, “The feedback–truth gap appears across learning systems”
rows.note: Representative run at the 46th percentile of gap magnitude across n = 90 model-noise configurations.
rows.check: The growing gap is reported correctly, but does not identify clean-example versus corrupted-example learning or establish perfect random-label fitting.

rows.subject: six architectures across five benchmark datasets
rows.operation_detail: Trained with synthetic symmetric label noise; measured gap prevalence across model-noise combinations.

conditions.value: six, including label smoothing, L2 regularization, and residual variants

rows.measure: Fraction of model-noise combinations with a positive gap
rows.value: The gap was observed in greater than 90% of model-noise combinations at 40% label noise.
rows.locator: Results, “The feedback–truth gap appears across learning systems”; Figure 2a
rows.note: Aggregate across model-noise combinations; Figure 2a separately reports prevalence across 90 conditions.
rows.check: Gap prevalence does not measure any version's outcome. The 90 conditions span three noise rates; the greater-than-90% result concerns the 40% subset.

rows.subject: six architectures across five benchmark datasets
rows.operation_detail: Trained across label-noise rates and measured the training-minus-validation gap.
rows.value: The gap disappeared completely when the label noise rate was 0%.
rows.locator: Results, “The feedback–truth gap appears across learning systems”; Extended Data Figs. 1 and 2
rows.note: The text reports this as an aggregate result across the tested settings.
rows.check: The stated disappearance of the gap under clean labels is accurately extracted, but does not establish good absolute generalization or perfect training fit.

rows.subject: dense baseline
rows.operation_detail: Applied as a noise-robust-method comparison on 30 OpenML datasets with 40% symmetric label noise.
rows.measure: Median AUGnorm; median T*; fraction with AUG > 0.005
rows.note: Table reports medians per dataset and fraction of datasets with a measurable gap.
rows.check: The table values are correct. These are gap summaries for a method comparison, not random-label fitting rates or convergence times.

rows.subject: sparse-residual
rows.operation_detail: Applied as a noise-robust-method comparison on 30 OpenML datasets with 40% symmetric label noise.
rows.measure: Median AUGnorm; median T*; fraction with AUG > 0.005
rows.note: The paper states that the gap is suppressed but not abolished across methods.
rows.check: The table values are correct. Suppression of a training–validation gap does not demonstrate prevention of random-label fitting.

rows.subject: co-teaching
rows.operation_detail: Applied as a noise-robust-method comparison on 30 OpenML datasets with 40% symmetric label noise.
rows.measure: Median AUGnorm; median T*; fraction with AUG > 0.005
rows.note: The paper states that the gap is suppressed but not abolished across methods.
rows.check: The table values are correct. Co-teaching gap suppression does not measure a claim version; it is also outside V5's named interventions.

rows.subject: forward loss correction
rows.operation_detail: Applied as a noise-robust-method comparison on 30 OpenML datasets with 40% symmetric label noise.
rows.measure: Median AUGnorm; median T*; fraction with AUG > 0.005
rows.note: The paper states that the gap is suppressed but not abolished across methods.
rows.check: The table values are correct. Loss-correction gap suppression does not measure a claim version; it is also outside V5's named interventions.

rows.subject: dense neural networks across 150 dataset–model pairs
rows.operation_detail: Related cumulative gap magnitude to validation accuracy under synthetic label noise.
rows.measure: Fixed-effects regression coefficient for AUGnorm predicting validation accuracy
rows.locator: Results, “The significance of the gap depends upon regulation”; Figure 3a
rows.note: The paper describes cumulative gap magnitude as a strong negative predictor of validation accuracy.
rows.check: The reported regression concerns gap–accuracy association, not perfect fitting or an accuracy trajectory across corruption rates.

rows.subject: dense and sparse-residual networks
rows.operation_detail: Related final train-validation gap to validation accuracy.
rows.measure: Spearman correlation between final train-validation gap and validation accuracy
rows.value: Dense networks: ρ = −0.74; ResEx networks: ρ = −0.37
rows.uncertainty: Dense: p-value not stated for this correlation; ResEx: p-value not stated
rows.note: Separate model-group correlations are reported; the ResEx association is described as attenuated.
rows.check: The reported correlations concern gap–accuracy association and do not establish any version's fitting or learning-order outcome.

rows.subject: sparse-residual networks
rows.operation_detail: Varied sparse-residual bottleneck strength α across configurations.
rows.baseline: Dense baseline has the largest gap and earliest onset.
rows.value: Both AUGnorm and T* increased monotonically with α (Spearman ρ = 1.0 for both metrics).
rows.locator: Results, “Regulation is tunable and dissociates pressure from recovery”; Figure 4a–b
rows.note: Increasing α weakens suppression; the text reports monotonicity across datasets with measurable gaps.
rows.check: The positive monotonicities are accurately transcribed, but the text is internally inconsistent: increasing T* with alpha means later onset at larger alpha, whereas the caption says stronger constraints delay onset. T* measures gap onset, not convergence time.

rows.subject: sparse-residual networks
rows.operation_detail: Compared test accuracy across bottleneck strengths and gap magnitudes.
rows.value: Test accuracy peaked at α = 0.1–0.25 and decreased at higher values.
rows.locator: Results, “Regulation is tunable and dissociates pressure from recovery”; Figure 4c
rows.note: The study reports a non-monotonic relationship, with maximal gap suppression not maximizing generalization.
rows.check: Test accuracy versus bottleneck strength does not measure a claim version. The main text gives a peak at alpha 0.1–0.25; the figure caption and supplementary methods specify 0.25.

rows.subject: sparse-residual versus dense baseline networks
rows.operation_detail: Compared test accuracy across 30 OpenML datasets under multiple noise rates.
rows.measure: Fraction of datasets where sparse bottlenecks improved accuracy
rows.value: 93% of datasets at 40% noise; median Δ = +3.28 pp.
rows.uncertainty: 95% binomial CI; bounds not stated for this 40% result in the figure text
rows.note: The advantage is described as noise-dependent.
rows.check: The values match Extended Data Figure 5, but are method-performance comparisons. Extended Data Table 2 separately reports a median accuracy improvement of 0.081 at 40% noise, rather than 3.28 percentage points; the summaries should not be conflated.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
